title: The Salt Road Cartographers
author: Liv Hartikainen
setting: Orrin, a continent whose land rearranges itself in the dark along a band called the Seam: a road ends at a cliff by morning, a lake wanders half a mile east, a village wakes beside a different river. The Cartographers' Guild of Karst Hollow sells the only trustworthy maps, redrawn each dawn by riders called Dawn-Surveyors. Salt caravans, ink-makers, rope-bridge towns, map-makers' superstitions (never draw a place you have not stood in; never name a place twice).
premise: Reet Sallik, 19, a junior surveyor with a perfect memory for ground and a stammer only when she lies, is the one person who notices that the Shifts follow a pattern: they match, with a delay, the Guild's master-atlas locked in the vault. Someone is altering the atlas and the land is obeying. Her mentor, Toomas Veskimae, the disgraced former Atlas-Keeper, is the obvious suspect and the only person who can help her. With a salt-caravan guard called Aino and an ink-maker's son, they cross the Seam to find where the Atlas gets its authority and why the land keeps promises made on paper. At the end Reet must draw, truthfully, a place that does not yet exist to save the town of Palu, and decide whether the Guild's power should survive.
pov: Close third person, past tense, alternating between Reet and Toomas.
tone: Warm, wry, adventurous, with real peril. Rich in map-lore and craft detail (inks, chains, plumb-lines, the grammar of contour). Found family. Humour in the caravan scenes.
names: Finnic/Estonian-flavoured invented names: Reet, Toomas, Aino, Veikko, Liisu, Mihkel, Kaie, Taavi. Place names invented in the same flavour (Karst Hollow, Palu, Haldja Ford). Keep diacritics out.
ending: Earned and bittersweet-hopeful. The Guild's monopoly is broken; maps begin to be made by asking the people who live there. A real cost is paid.

title: The Tin Dragon's Apprentice
author: Corwen Pell
setting: Gantry, a smoke-and-slate port city on a brackish estuary where spell-engineers and boiler-wrights share guild halls. The city's heat and light come from Old Ferrous, a forty-foot mechanical dragon asleep in the Furnace Cathedral, fed coal and charm for two hundred years. Brass, riveted pipes, gaslight, tide-clocks, canal barges, pigeon post, soot-snow.
premise: Odile Marchetti, 16, a canal-boat mechanic's daughter, is made apprentice to the Dragon-Warden, a gruff ex-soldier called Bastien Orlowe, only because three better candidates quit. Old Ferrous is waking, and what wakes is not an engine but a mind: hungry, curious and very old, which prefers talking to Odile because she asks questions instead of giving orders. The Fuel Commissioner wants the dragon broken up for scrap and power; the guilds want it kept asleep; the dragon wants to see the sea. A heist, a flood, a trial, and a friendship.
pov: First person, past tense, Odile: funny, practical, sharp-eyed, furious at being called 'dear'.
tone: Warm, quick, witty and adventurous. Middle-grade-adjacent heart but real stakes. Mechanical detail is precise, tactile and fun. A comic supporting cast.
names: Franco-Italian and Mitteleuropean flavour: Odile, Bastien, Ottoline, Casimir, Fenwick, Tibor, Marguerite, Lorcan, Pim (a messenger boy), Commissioner Hartwell Gast.
ending: Triumphant and tender. The dragon reaches the sea, and leaves its heart-fire to the city on new terms.

title: The River That Remembered
author: Sovanna Idris
setting: The Lower Reaches, a delta kingdom of a thousand channels, stilt-houses and floating markets. Its great river, the Amaru, carries the memories of everyone who drowns in it and gives them back as dreams to those who drink. Ferry-guilds hold sacred neutrality; the rains are late; salt creeps upriver; the Water-Lords' dams hold back the highland flood-pulse.
premise: Thida Vorn, 41, a ferrywoman who has carried the belongings of the dead downriver for twenty years and has never drunk the water since she lost her daughter to it, is hired by a prince's widow to carry one sealed jar upriver to the source. The jar holds a drowned man's memory that would prove the old king's death was no accident and that the dams are killing the river. With a boy who maps channels, her late husband's cousin, and a river-priest who has stopped believing, Thida goes upriver against the season while the river itself answers questions the way memory does: sideways.
pov: Close third person, present tense, Thida, with short interludes in the river's own voice (second person, 'you').
tone: Lyrical but grounded and unsentimental. Ferrying as skilled work. Grief carried not dwelt on. Slow-burning with escalating danger from the Water-Lords' enforcers. Some dry humour from the boy.
names: Invented names with a flavour of the Mekong and Niger deltas: Thida, Sovann, Ketema, Oluwa, Bakary, Channary, Dara, Ife. Place names as river words: the Amaru, Low Tamber, Nine Sluices, the Mother Gate.
ending: The dams are broken on Thida's terms, at a price. The river gives her daughter's memory back to her. Release, not triumph.

title: Murder at the Marigold Bindery
author: Hester Pryce-Lowell
setting: Trevenna, a Cornish fishing village, summer 1989. The Marigold Bindery is a small hand-bookbinding workshop above the harbour: an iron hand-press, a nipping press, paste pots, bone folders, a cat called Quire. Also the pub (The Drowned Lantern), the chapel, the Women's Institute, the regatta, the big house (Penhallow Court), tourists, and a three-day antiquarian book fair in the church hall.
premise: Dorothea 'Dot' Pellow, 58, widowed bookbinder and reluctant amateur sleuth, finds the village's rare-book collector and regatta chairman Aubrey Trevithick dead in her press room during the book fair, a half-sewn manuscript on the bench with its endpapers torn out. Because she can read how a book was made (thread, paste, repairs, paper stock, the hand of the binder) she can tell that the manuscript has been rebound twice and its contents swapped. Fair-play clues rooted in the craft; eight suspects; two more crimes; a constable who is her nephew's ex-girlfriend; a pub quiz; a regatta that ends in a reveal.
pov: First person, past tense, Dot: dry, wry, practical, with asides about binding and about being invisible at fifty-eight.
tone: Cosy but not twee. Sharp social comedy, real grief, village secrets. A genuine fair-play puzzle with a reveal in the last chapters and clues a careful reader can catch.
names: Cornish and English: Dot Pellow, Aubrey Trevithick, Jago Rowe, Morwenna Hext, Constable Demelza Kitto, the Reverend Arthur Nance, Tamsin Bray, a Dutch dealer Pieter de Vries.
ending: Justice, with a twist that recasts a harmless-seeming early scene. Dot takes on an apprentice.

title: The Ninth Floor
author: Dominic Vasko
setting: Port Calder, a fictional West Coast shipping city, November 1952: fog, cranes, union halls, cheap hotels, neon, rain. The Harbor Hotel has eight floors on the plans and eight buttons in the elevator.
premise: Ruth Szymanski, 36, a former police dispatcher turned private investigator, is hired by a hotel night clerk to find out why a dead guest was found on the ninth floor of a building that only has eight. The trail runs through dock unions, a missing ship's manifest, a jazz singer with a false name, a ledger kept in a Polish-language prayer book, and a respectable councilman who owns the pier. Every client lies; Ruth lies back; a second body turns up in the elevator shaft.
pov: First person, past tense, Ruth: laconic and wry, tough without being a cartoon, notices hands and shoes. Period slang used sparingly and accurately.
tone: Noir: moody, rain-soaked, morally grey, crisp short chapters, dry humour, no cheap misery. Plot is tight and clues are fair.
names: 1950s American mix (Polish, Irish, Chinese, Italian, Black American): Ruth Szymanski, Ambrose Quill, Detective Sergeant Frank Dolan, Yvette Marchand (the singer), Councilman Everett Plum, hotel clerk Tadeusz 'Teddy' Wozniak, Lucille Fong.
ending: Solved at a cost. Ruth keeps the prayer book.

title: The Observatory at Verglas
author: Clemence Aubry
setting: February 1936. The Observatoire du Verglas, a private astronomical station at 3,100 metres on a French-Italian Alpine ridge, reached only by a cable car that stops in a storm. A telescope dome, instruments, a kitchen, a library, a radio, a winter crew of nine. Europe is uneasy, but up here it is snow and the sky.
premise: A storm closes the cable. The Director is found dead in the dome beneath the great telescope, shot with a gun nobody at the station owns, in a room locked from inside. Among those trapped: Helene Kranz, a retired Vienna policewoman who came to give a lecture; an Italian physicist; a young Welsh computer (a human calculator); an Armenian cook; a Swiss meteorologist; a priest who studies eclipses. As the storm lengthens, comfort gives way to fear, the radio is smashed, and the Director's last observation log turns out to have been altered. The solution depends on astronomy: time, parallax and how a dome turns.
pov: Close third person, past tense, rotating across four viewpoints (Helene and three others).
tone: Classic puzzle in elegant prose: warm characters, real cold, a creeping dread, a clue trail a careful reader can follow. The astronomy is accurate and explained through character.
names: Franco-Italian-Swiss-Welsh-Armenian mix: Helene Kranz, Aurelio Bassi, Gwenllian 'Gwen' Pryor, Araxie Demirjian, Ueli Brunner, Father Anselm Roux, Director Maxime Delacroix-Lorin.
ending: The reveal in the dome at dawn, with a moral cost that is not wholly resolved.

title: Zero-Day Lullaby
author: Kasper Lindahl
setting: Present day, winter. Tallinn (the Old Town and the tech district), a children's hospital network, Singapore data centres, a Lagos fintech, a Helsinki summit, an overnight ferry across the Gulf of Finland. Incident-response war rooms, smart speakers, hospital IT.
premise: Ilse Kantor, 38, an incident responder at a small Tallinn firm, is called to the children's hospital after the neonatal ward's smart speakers hum the same lullaby at 3 a.m. The lullaby is the exfiltration channel of a state-grade implant stealing the medical records of the children of government ministers across six countries. As she traces it, her firm's founder is murdered, her own phone is bugged, and the people hunting the implant are as dangerous as the people who wrote it. Short, ticking chapters and a countdown to the Helsinki summit.
pov: Close third person, present tense, mainly Ilse, with short interludes from a hunter known as the Courier and from a hospital nurse, Pille.
tone: Pacey, technically credible, never lecturing. Paranoia, ferries, cold. Humane: children are never harmed on the page.
names: Estonian, Finnish, Singaporean and Nigerian mix: Ilse Kantor, Pille Rebane, Jaan Tamm, Dr Mei Lin Ong, Chidi Abara, Colonel Aleksei Novik. Use a fictional agency ('the Directorate') and no real intelligence services.
ending: A smart, costly victory. Ilse goes public. Some ambiguity remains about who else was listening.

title: The Quiet Witness
author: Rosalind Tamayo
setting: Present-day Newark, New Jersey: the federal courthouse, cheap lunch counters, a Dominican bakery in the Ironbound, the commuter rail to New York, the Meadowlands in fog. A racketeering trial against a port freight company.
premise: Marisol Quintanilla, 44, a freelance Spanish-English court interpreter, is sworn to faithfulness and neutrality. During a recess she overhears, through a thin wall and in a regional Spanish the lawyers do not realise she knows, a defence lawyer coaching the prosecution's star witness to lie. If she speaks she breaks her oath of confidentiality and perhaps ends her career; if she stays silent a man will go to prison for life. She starts quietly checking facts; someone notices. Cat and mouse with a private investigator, a federal marshal, and her estranged brother, who works at the port.
pov: Close third person, past tense, Marisol, with a few chapters from the prosecutor Dana Whitcomb and from the witness, Rigoberto 'Rigo' Salas.
tone: Taut, grounded, workplace-realistic. The craft of interpreting is shown in detail (consecutive and simultaneous, register, untranslatable words). Slow-tightening dread with moral gravity.
names: Dominican-American, Puerto Rican, Irish-American, Black American and Gujarati-American court staff: Marisol Quintanilla, Rigoberto Salas, Dana Whitcomb, Judge Anselm Okoro, defence lawyer Vincent Lazzaro, Marshal Priya Desai, her brother Teo.
ending: She testifies about what she heard, at a price. The profession's rules are questioned and she is not destroyed.

title: What the Peat Kept
author: Declan Furey
setting: A raised bog in the Irish midlands, autumn 1974: turf-cutting by hand, a townland of seven families, the Angelus bell, the machines of the national peat board at the far edge, a ruined ancient cooking-pit, mist. A parish where the priest is respected and the old customs are quietly kept.
premise: The Dolan family cuts turf for the winter. Under four feet of peat the slean strikes a body: a man, long dead, tanned and whole, with a rope around his neck and a twist of hair in his fist. The guards come and go; the museum will collect him in a fortnight. But the bog begins to want something back. Small wrongs multiply: black water in dry fields, a neighbour sleepwalking to the cutting, the dead man's face in the turf stack, and the youngest, Nuala, 9, says the man has asked her to keep him company. What the bog kept, and why, is tied to a pact the townland's grandparents made.
pov: Close third person, past tense, rotating among five of the Dolans and a neighbour. Creeping and quiet, with no cheap jump scares.
tone: Slow dread, rural realism, dry Irish humour, grief. Horror from implication and custom. A few moments of real fear. The ending hurts.
names: Irish midlands: Brid Dolan, Mattie Dolan, Nuala, Tadhg, Father Colm Heffernan, Peg Gorman, Eamon Brophy, Garda Sergeant Noel Quirke. Keep Irish-language words few and correct.
ending: The pact is honoured in a way that costs the family. A quiet, ambiguous coda.

title: Unit 4B Does Not Exist
author: Tobias Nwosu
setting: Harwick Terrace, a mid-rise rental building on 31st Street in an unnamed mid-sized American city; the property-management office, rent rolls, elevators, laundry room, tenant group chat. Present day, a wet autumn.
premise: Dev Mahajan, 29, a data-entry clerk at Corvane Property Group, finds that apartment 4B appears on the rent roll with a paying tenant but has no floor plan, no door and no building permit. He walks the fourth floor: 4A, then 4C. He starts counting his steps. Tenants speak about 4B as if they know it. He is told to delete the row; he doesn't. The more he investigates, the more the building rearranges itself around him, and the more his own life (his flat, his sister, his job) starts to lose its edges.
pov: First person, past tense, Dev: anxious, funny, observant. Documents (emails, notes, listings, a lease) are interleaved with the narrative as block quotes (lines starting with > ).
tone: Uncanny, cumulative, claustrophobic. Office comedy that curdles into dread. Clean plain prose. Fear arises from bureaucracy and almost-normal details.
names: South Asian-American, Nigerian-American, Latino, Korean-American, white working-class mix: Dev Mahajan, Chioma Eze (4A), Rafael 'Rafa' Ibarra (maintenance), Zofia Baran (3rd floor), manager Noreen Whitmore, his sister Anjali, tenant Mr Ptolemy Grieve.
ending: Dev makes a choice about the room. Disturbing and quietly sad.

title: A Fortnight of Rain in Kilmuir
author: Eilidh Rankin
setting: Kilmuir, a fictional island in the Inner Hebrides, present day, in a very rainy June: a ferry that runs when the wind allows, a one-room shop and post office, a ceilidh hall, peat smoke, midges, the Gaelic and English of the island.
premise: Nell Okoye-Brandt, 34, a burned-out London sound engineer, takes a fortnight's job recording the island's elderly Gaelic singers for a national archive, and is stranded when the ferry stops. Calum MacAskill, 37, the island's widowed ferry skipper and part-time mechanic, is the only person with a boat, a van and a spare room. Their fortnight stretches to a month of weather, work and neighbours with opinions. Shared silence, shared recordings, two people who have each decided they are done with starting over. Calum has a recording of his late wife that he cannot bear to play.
pov: Close third person, past tense, alternating Nell and Calum.
tone: Warm, funny, wistful; the weather as a character; the sound of things. Closed-door: kisses only. Real obstacles (grief, a London job offer, island life), not manufactured misunderstandings.
names: Scottish Hebridean and British-Nigerian: Nell Okoye-Brandt, Calum MacAskill, Morag, old Seonaidh, Iseabail, the minister Rev. Donald Iain. Keep Gaelic phrases few and correct.
ending: She stays on new terms. The last chapter is a song.

title: The Marquess's Misprint
author: Georgiana Fenwick
setting: London and Kent, 1816, the Season, the year without a summer: cold wet June, failed harvests, rain at every garden party. The print shops of Paternoster Row, a scandal sheet called The Town Crier, assemblies, a country-house party, a printer's yard with an Albion press.
premise: One misprinted line in the Gazette announces the engagement of Julian, Marquess of Stanmere, to 'Miss W. Pargeter of Paternoster Row.' There is no such engagement, but there is a Winifred Pargeter, 26, a printer's daughter who set the type and made the error. The Marquess, hunted by matchmakers and his own fear of marriage, is tempted to let it stand for the Season; Winifred's father's press faces ruin if the error is exposed. Fake engagement, a rival printer, a fierce dowager aunt, a runaway press, and a dinner party at which Winifred outshines everyone.
pov: An arch third-person narrator with an amused, slightly omniscient voice who occasionally addresses the reader, past tense. Mainly Winifred and Julian.
tone: Witty and warm, with period-accurate diction and no parody. Romantic and funny, closed-door. Printing-trade detail (composing stick, forme, ink balls, the Albion press).
names: Regency English: Winifred Pargeter, Julian Stanmere, Lady Constance Dyer (the aunt), Barnaby Pargeter (her father), Mr Hector Lovejoy (rival printer), Lord Rupert Tremayne (rival suitor), Miss Agnes Fell (companion).
ending: The record is set straight in print, publicly. A wedding done the proper way.

title: The Cold Open
author: Jules Ferreira
setting: Present day, a Cleveland winter: a failing AM station called KLZ 1340 'The Lake' in an old building on Euclid Avenue, lake-effect snow, diners, an unsold broadcast tower. The station is about to be sold.
premise: Wendell 'Dell' Achterberg, 41, host of the beloved quiet-voiced overnight show Night Shift, is made to share the studio with Priya Raman, 34, a high-energy podcaster brought in by the new owners to 'modernise' the slot. They loathe each other on air, and the audience adores it. Enemies to lovers over a winter of snowstorms, a prank war, a listener who calls every night, a stolen reel-to-reel tape, a fundraiser, and a decision about letting the station be sold.
pov: First person, past tense, alternating between Dell and Priya. The speaker must be clear from the first line of each chapter (there are no headings inside the text). Distinct voices: Dell is dry, melancholy and old-souled; Priya is fast, funny and anxious.
tone: Banter-forward romantic comedy with heart. Radio craft in detail. Closed-door. No cheating, no cartoon villains. The nightly caller subplot ends in a sweet reveal.
names: Midwestern American with Gujarati-American and Polish-American: Dell Achterberg, Priya Raman, station manager Rosemary 'Ro' Pavlik, engineer Hakeem Boateng, caller 'Wanda from Parma', the owners' rep Brent Whitlock.
ending: They save the station as a listener co-op. The last chapter is the last cold open.

title: The Long Quiet
author: Pavel Soderquist
setting: The ship Carrack Hesper, six generations into a 214-year voyage: three spin-habitats around a central spine, eleven thousand people, a constant 40 Hz hum from the drive. Orchard Deck, the Hydroponic Halls, Lamplighter Ring, the Council of Stewards, the Remembrancers who keep the lore of Earth.
premise: Everyone aboard Hesper has lived inside the engine's hum. Then, on an ordinary Tuesday, it stops. Acoustic engineer Tomasz Adeyemi-Lindqvist, 33, a 'keeper of silences' whose job is tuning the ship's sound, is the first to realise that the engine has not failed: something is listening. In the silence, old rumours, buried archives and class resentments rise. A mutiny on the lower decks; a Steward who wants to turn the ship; a child who talks to the walls.
pov: Close third person, past tense, rotating among five viewpoints: Tomasz; Steward Ines Okonkwo-Reyes; the Remembrancer Yoshiko; a Deck Four mechanic, Bram; and the child Pip.
tone: Humane, mysterious, politically aware. Sound design treated as science. Mid-paced with a rising crisis. Awe and fear in equal measure.
names: Future-global mixed names: Tomasz Adeyemi-Lindqvist, Ines Okonkwo-Reyes, Yoshiko Haverford, Bram Kowalczyk, Pip, Steward Sunniva Achebe-Lund.
ending: A revelation about what was listening, resolved humanely, with the ship changed for good.

title: Seawall
author: Anika Raghunathan
setting: 2071. Tamarind Delta, a fictional delta megacity of nineteen million on a vast low coast, behind a 140-kilometre seawall. Monsoon surge season; floating markets in flooded districts; pump-houses, relocation camps, municipal politics, repair drones, a drowned old city beneath the water.
premise: Municipal engineer Kavya Menon-Iyer, 39, is Deputy Chief of Seawall Section Nine. A storm surge forecast ten days out will test the wall with a surge the models say it cannot withstand. The city administrator wants the forecast kept quiet to avoid panic; the contractor wants to cut corners; the district councils want to flood the poor wards to spare the rich ones. Kavya fights the clock with a ragtag crew, an old pumping-station operator, and a teenager who has made a flood map from children's drone footage. Ten days, ten escalating decisions.
pov: First person, present tense, Kavya: practical, sardonic, exhausted. Chapters carry the day countdown only in the first sentence, not as a heading.
tone: Engineering procedural with humane stakes, hopeful but unsparing. Moral choices at scale. Technical detail made accessible. No villain monologues.
names: South Indian, Bengali, Sri Lankan, Filipino and Nigerian mix: Kavya Menon-Iyer, Tariq Hossain, Administrator Dilhani Wickramasinghe, old Mr Anand, the teenager Liyana, contractor Ricardo Santos.
ending: A partial victory: the wall holds in part, one district chooses to flood, and rebuilding begins.

title: Vessel Nine
author: Yusra Haldane
setting: 2047. Nine objects have entered orbit. One, Vessel Nine, has come down in the Kerguelen Islands, in the sub-Antarctic Indian Ocean, near an international research station: wind, sleds, kelp, penguins, sheet-metal huts, an enormous tank of seawater in which the visitors communicate by pulses of pressure and temperature.
premise: Dr Halima Reyes-Okafor, 47, a field linguist who documented the last speakers of dying languages, is flown in to decipher Vessel Nine's 'speech'. Her method is patient fieldwork, not code-breaking: sit, give, ask, make mistakes. Governments want to know 'what they want' within weeks. She and her team discover that the visitors have no word for 'I' or 'you', and she must work out what to do when a message from Vessel Nine is a question and the wrong answer is irreversible.
pov: Close third person, past tense, Halima, interleaved with field-note and transcript excerpts set as block quotes (lines starting with > ).
tone: Intelligent, patient, awestruck and human. Fieldwork detail. Tension comes from politics and doubt rather than from the aliens. The emotional core is her late father's language.
names: A mixed international team: Halima Reyes-Okafor, Dr Ewan Menzies, Captain Ioana Petrescu, the mathematician Daiki Mori, Ambassador Beatrice Lemaire, the junior translator Sipho.
ending: She answers with the truth about uncertainty. Contact is established. Bittersweet, with a cost.

title: After the Shaking
author: Lourdes Quintela
setting: Lisbon from the morning of All Saints' Day, 1 November 1755, through the following year: the earthquake, the fires and the tidal wave; the ruins of the lower city; tent camps in the hills; the confusion of church and crown; the rebuilding on a grid; the printers' quarter, the English merchants, convents, the Tagus. Real history is the backdrop. Historical figures are seen only at a distance.
premise: Ines Carvalhal, 19, the daughter of a printer in the Rua dos Douradores, survives the earthquake in her cellar and climbs out to find the press buried and her brother Rodrigo missing. She searches the ruins, joins a tent hospital run by an English merchant's quarrelsome wife and a defrocked friar, learns to read the new lists of the dead and the found, and discovers that her father's press printed a pamphlet that powerful people want destroyed.
pov: Close third person, past tense, Ines, with occasional letters from Rodrigo.
tone: Humane, vivid, unflinching about disaster without wallowing. Period detail worn lightly. Moral questions about blame, providence and rebuilding. Hope in work.
names: Portuguese and English of the eighteenth century: Ines Carvalhal, Rodrigo, Brother Agostinho, Mrs Harriet Lowther (English), Dom Fernao, Joana the laundress, Father Anselmo.
ending: She prints something new from a salvaged press. Rodrigo is found, alive but changed.

title: Forty Below
author: Wilhelmina Strand
setting: Dawson City, Yukon, winter of 1898-99: a boom town of tents and log saloons, mud turned to ice, forty-below nights, dog teams, sourdoughs, the North-West Mounted Police, claims on Bonanza and Eldorado creeks, dance halls, a town always one stove away from fire, river steamers frozen in.
premise: Constance 'Connie' Rudd, 31, a widowed typesetter from Seattle, arrives with a hand-press in pieces and starts a four-page weekly, the Dawson Dispatch, determined to print the truth. The truth is a claim-jumping ring, a faked assay, a missing partner, and a Mountie who is more honest than he looks. A winter, a fire, and a race by dog team along a hundred miles of river ice to file a claim before the registry closes.
pov: Close third person, past tense, Connie. Each chapter may open with a short invented newspaper clipping set as a block quote (lines starting with > ).
tone: Robust, funny, tough and humane. Adventure with real cold. Frontier slang used lightly. Honest about the harm done to the Indigenous Han people, whose land the town stands on.
names: Settlers and the Han: Connie Rudd, Sergeant Alasdair Moffat (NWMP), 'Cuthbert' Tull (the claim shark), Hannah Beaumont (the cook), and Martha, a Han woman who is a skilled dog-driver and interpreter with her own aims and dignity. No stereotypes; do not invent native-sounding words; give Martha an ordinary English name and a plain, particular life.
ending: The paper prints the truth. Connie stays. It costs her.

title: The Summer We Sold the House
author: Frances Adeyemi
setting: Lorain, Ohio, July: a 1962 brick foursquare on a street called Pearl, a backyard garden of tomatoes and a cherry tree, a sewing room, a basement full of forty years, Lake Erie, Fourth of July fireworks, a church fish fry, the realtor's sign.
premise: Three adult siblings come home to clear the house of their widowed mother, Odessa Adeyemi-Prewitt, 76, who is showing the early signs of dementia and must move into assisted living; the house has to be sold in six weeks. Tunde, 46, eldest, a financial planner and a controller; Sade, 41, a nurse in Atlanta, resentful; Remi, 35, the youngest, a musician, unreliable. Boxes open old arguments; each sibling has a secret; their mother's lucid moments and her new habit of giving things away to neighbours reshape the summer. A garden party ends it.
pov: Rotating first person, past tense, among the three siblings; each chapter opens with the sibling's name as its first words so the reader knows whose voice it is. Distinct voices.
tone: Literary, warm, funny and sad. Domestic detail. No melodrama. Each chapter is built around an object found in the house.
names: Nigerian-American (Yoruba) and Black Midwestern: Tunde, Sade, Remi, their mother Odessa, the neighbour Mr Valentine Okafor, Pastor Greene, realtor Brenda Kowalski, Tunde's daughter Imani.
ending: The house is sold, their mother settled, the siblings changed toward each other. The cherry tree.

title: Everyone Here Is Fine
author: Remy Laframboise
setting: Pelletier Bend, a fictional town of 1,140 people in Saskatchewan, October: a grain elevator, the curling rink, the Legion hall, the Co-op, a community theatre in the old Lutheran church, the town's centennial pageant, minus-twelve mornings, hockey, perogies, rural-municipality politics.
premise: Gabe Lefebvre, 34, comes home from Toronto after his food-delivery startup collapses, and is conscripted by his mother to direct the town's centennial pageant: a ninety-minute historical revue to be staged in three weeks with a cast of thirty-one non-actors, including a retired judge cast as a bison. Everyone insists they are fine; no one is. The pageant becomes a ledger of the town's secrets: a dispute over a stolen sculpture, a Metis family whose chapter of local history the official script left out, a lost love, and a feud between the curling club and the Legion.
pov: First person, past tense, Gabe: deadpan, self-deprecating, observant. Short scenes and running jokes.
tone: Comic with heart, true to prairie small-town life, affectionate and never mocking. Real emotion arrives in the last act.
names: Prairie Canadian: Gabe Lefebvre, his mother Colette, Dolores Kowalchuk (stage manager), Judge Harold Thorsteinson (the bison), Maurice Desjarlais (a Metis elder), Rosalie Dumont (his ex).
ending: Pageant night: chaos and grace. Gabe stays through the spring.
